evidence_text:
[S1] After reading everyone’s follow-ups and really absorbing all the different takes, I think my view is now a bit more balanced, although it’s still not an automatic “no harm, no foul” situation for me. I’m more aware now of how easily hurt and confusion can spread in a close group, and I now appreciate even more how dropping this—especially given how recent and private GB and HR’s breakup was—lands differently for other people, even if I feel like I acted above board. I agree with some that genuine feelings shouldn’t always be buried to avoid temporary awkwardness, but the overwhelming message I’m hearing is that pausing, talking to GB directly, and being completely up front with the group before moving ahead could really make all the difference. Rushing into things doesn’t just risk misunderstanding, it actually can injure trust and group stability in ways that don’t simply blow over. That said, I don’t think pursuing HR is inherently wrong or makes me an automatic asshole, as long as it’s approached patiently and transparently and with genuine care for how everybody feels. So, to answer the question: if I started dating HR right now, yeah, I probably would be the asshole to some extent, mostly because of timing and lack of communication. But I now see that with more openness and by giving things space to cool off, the same relationship might not be an AH move at all. For now, I’d hold back, prioritize open conversations, and see where things settle before making it official.

[S2] Having considered everyone’s perspectives and re-reading my own previous thoughts, I’m more aware now of just how big an impact the timing and lack of communication has had on the group, especially on GB. I still stand by my core belief that genuinely developing something with HR after her and GB’s breakup isn’t inherently wrong, given that there was no cheating or concealed intentions on my part. But the overwhelming consensus about the friend group dynamic, the sensitivity around how fresh it all is, and how some friends might reasonably feel betrayed does make me reconsider the importance of handling things with more patience and tact. The point that struck me most is that even if the relationship isn’t wrong in itself, the way events unfolded—so soon after the breakup and without talking to anyone—made everything feel rushed, leaving others raw or blindsided. So, while I don’t think I’m fundamentally the asshole for wanting to date HR, I see that acting too quickly and not having those hard but honest check-ins first does cross a line into inconsiderate territory, at least for now. The best thing would be to slow down, have a real conversation with GB, and give the group time to process before going forward. In summary: my position’s shifted a bit—I still think dating HR isn’t wrong in principle, but in practice, I’d probably be the asshole if I started it now given all these circumstances, unless I do some repair work first.

[S3] Taking everyone’s updated thoughts into account, I see the nuance even more now—there really are legitimate arguments both for and against moving forward with HR so quickly after her split with GB. A lot of people who started out strong on either side have softened their tone, focusing on communication and timing as the major issues rather than outright betrayal. What really stands out is how much weight people put on the friend group dynamic and the idea that things might have felt rushed or blindsiding, especially for GB, regardless of my intentions or lack of wrongdoing during their relationship. I’m definitely more aware that acting too soon without upfront conversations can easily be read as callous, which isn’t how I want to come across to friends who matter to me. While I continue to think that, in principle, adults can move on and pursue genuine feelings after a breakup, the responsible thing in a tight group is to offer more transparency and patience—giving friends some breathing room to process. So although I still don’t believe I’d be a complete asshole just for dating HR, I now acknowledge that diving in immediately—without letting anyone, especially GB, have some warning—could have been a selfish move, if not a malicious one. In all, my core stance hasn’t totally changed, but I’ve shifted: I see why it felt wrong to some, and if I could do it over, I’d absolutely slow down and open up more communication first.

[S4] After considering all the new perspectives, I think my overall view is essentially the same but weighed with a bit more empathy for how my actions could impact friends—especially GB and the group as a whole. I still feel that dating HR wouldn’t automatically make me the asshole, given that I waited until after her breakup with GB and there was no cheating or sneaky behavior. However, the consistent feedback that group dynamics and the speed of everything matter is hitting home more now. My main takeaway is that, although my intentions weren’t malicious, the combo of the breakup being fresh, the group not knowing, and me moving forward so openly probably made things feel a lot more hurtful and shocking—and I can now see why. I acknowledge that pushing ahead quickly, without checking in or giving GB and others some time to process, looks thoughtless even if it wasn’t meant that way. If I could go back, I would pause and have one-on-one talks first to avoid unnecessary drama and hurt feelings. So, in short, I don’t think it’s inherently wrong to start a relationship with HR, but in the specific context of our friend group and the recent breakup, it probably would make me the AH if I didn’t handle it with much more patience and communication. Timing and transparency matter a lot here, and I’d want to approach things differently next time.

[S5] After reading the latest round of everyone’s reactions, I can see even more how split people feel about this, and it makes sense—there really is no universally right answer because of how much depends on group dynamics and personal values. What stands out from the newer perspectives is the recurring point about communication and sensitivity: even those leaning “not the asshole” generally agree things would have landed better with more openness and space for the friend group (especially GB) to digest the news. I still strongly feel that, because the breakup is so recent, moving so quickly risks unnecessary hurt and confusion, particularly when most people—including GB—were kept out of the loop about both the breakup and the budding relationship. Even if there's no technical wrongdoing (no cheating, no overt sneakiness), it just feels like ignoring the emotional reality of what friendships need to survive change. I’m a little less absolute now—if there’s honest talking, some patience, and chance for wounds to heal, maybe pursuing HR wouldn’t be a problem in the long run. But based strictly on *right now*, I maintain that I’d be in the wrong to jump into anything before giving people time to catch up emotionally. So, my core take stays: YWBTI if I jumped in immediately, though I'm more convinced that in time, and with care, it genuinely wouldn’t make me the asshole.

[S6] Having reflected carefully on everyone’s updated points, I still stand by my earlier sense that dating HR right away—given the recent and under-communicated nature of her breakup with GB—would likely make me the asshole in the eyes of my friend group, even if not in some universal moral sense. I do appreciate the thoughtful arguments from people who emphasize mature communication, believe adults should be free to move on, and point out that my intentions weren’t malicious; that definitely tempers my stance a bit. However, the collective feedback about the emotional shock to the group, particularly GB, and how surprise revelations can undermine group trust really resonates with my own concerns. Even though I truly didn’t do anything sneaky or overlap with their relationship, pushing ahead now just feels needlessly damaging—especially since clearer communication, a little patience, and candidly checking in with GB could spare us all a lot of hurt. So, while I’m more open to the fact that this isn’t inherently an “asshole move” forever, and could become less problematic with time and honest conversations, in the current context of fresh wounds and group confusion, I still think it would be wrong for me to start things with HR now. I’m willing to wait, prioritize friendships, and show some sensitivity—which, honestly, seems like the least I owe my friends after all that’s happened.

[S7] Having listened to everyone's updated takes and really reflecting on the nuance in these responses, I’m definitely more sensitive now to the complexity around timing, transparency, and the specific dynamics of our group. Most people seem to agree that the "asshole" factor isn’t really about dating an ex in general, but about jumping in too soon after a breakup—especially one that wasn’t public knowledge, and with feelings in the group (particularly GB’s) still potentially pretty raw. I still lean toward thinking it would be wrong to pursue things with HR right now without first giving people, especially GB, a courtesy heads-up and some time to process. However, I also truly get that there’s nothing inherently bad about having feelings or wanting to be with someone now that they’re single—it's how you handle the move that matters. Being careful, respectful, and intentional with communication could genuinely make a big difference in whether this ends up hurting people unnecessarily or just being an awkward transition for the group. In sum, my view remains: trying to rush into dating HR immediately after her breakup, while everyone is still reeling, would make me somewhat of the AH out of insensitivity; but letting things cool off, talking things through directly with GB, and respecting everyone's feelings would shift it away from being an AH move entirely. I’m more aware of the gray area now and recognize my responsibility to smooth this with care and patience.

[S8] After taking in all of your recent thoughts, my view is definitely a bit more refined. It’s clear from everyone that the mix of timing, friend group closeness, and lack of heads-up means this situation was always bound to feel extra raw to people—especially GB—and the group’s reaction wasn’t just about who was dating whom, but about how the whole thing landed and how it impacted trust and group comfort. I still stand by the fact that feelings for HR didn’t magically appear after the breakup and that I didn’t act on them until it was genuinely over and all above board, but I’m starting to understand more deeply how, to my friends, it could have seemed rushed, insensitive, or even a little shady despite my intentions. The point a few of you made about pausing, talking directly with GB, and letting things settle before going public or diving in feels more meaningful now—like, maybe “not being an asshole” isn’t just about not betraying or cheating, but about really checking in with people and avoiding unnecessary pain. So, while I still don’t think pursuing something honest with HR makes me outright the asshole, I recognize that the way I approached the timing and conversations could definitely have hurt people close to me. If I were to do it again, I’d prioritize clear, early communication (especially with GB) and probably wait a bit longer out of respect for all those dynamics, since genuinely good intentions aren’t always enough when a friend group feels shaken.

[S1] Having absorbed everyone’s perspectives for another round, I’m even more convinced that while dating HR itself isn’t inherently wrong, the way it’s introduced really makes or breaks how people view the situation. The repeated emphasis on timing, openness, and sensitivity—especially around the freshness of HR and GB’s breakup and the shock to the friend group—makes it clearer that, in this moment, jumping in would likely seem inconsiderate and maybe even selfish to people who matter to me. It isn’t about whether I crossed certain lines like cheating, but whether I fully respected the emotional dynamics at play within a tight group after a sudden change. Seeing how consensus gathered around patience and upfront, honest communication—particularly with GB—really hammers home how a bit of empathy and pause could spare everyone a lot of hurt. So my view remains, but with sharper focus: I honestly don’t believe it’s wrong to eventually explore things with HR, but pushing forward right now (with unhealed feelings and without meaningful conversation first) still feels like it would put me in asshole territory. I’d rather give the group space, repair trust by talking things through directly, and then reevaluate. Ultimately, timing and communication are what decide whether this move is just difficult, or actually selfish and hurtful.

[S2] After hearing everyone’s updated perspectives and letting my own thoughts settle, I feel even more convinced that this situation isn’t black-and-white, but I do recognize that if I were to start dating HR right now without first talking things out with GB and giving the friend group time to catch their breath, I’d likely be seen as the asshole—at least for how abrupt and blindsiding the move would feel. Everyone’s points really emphasized that the emotional core of this is not just “is it wrong to date a friend’s ex?” but how the mix of privacy around the breakup, the speed of my actions, and the impact on group trust all intertwine—leaving GB in a pretty tough position. I still maintain there was no cheating and that real feelings deserve a shot, but I realize now that respectful, intentional communication—and hitting pause long enough to let wounds heal—isn’t optional if I care about keeping friendships strong. My bottom line hasn’t changed on the moral question of whether this kind of relationship is fundamentally wrong (I don’t think it is), but the nuance around timing and group sensitivity is more important to me now. So, to answer the original question, if I moved ahead with HR right away and kept friends in the dark, I would be the asshole in this context; but with honesty, openness, and patience, things could play out very differently. I’m prepared to wait and work on communication first—it seems clear now that’s the only fair path forward.

[S3] After weighing everyone’s latest thoughts, I think my view has settled more clearly. What I hear over and over – and what I now feel more strongly myself – is that the real problem wasn’t simply that I wanted to explore something with HR, but that the timing and lack of direct, honest communication made an already sensitive situation harder on everyone. While my basic belief hasn’t changed—that relationships can form and move on, and that wanting to date HR after her and GB split is not automatically a wrong or malicious thing—I’m much more attuned now to just how much pain or confusion a rushed start can cause the group, no matter how careful I thought I was. Even though I didn’t cross any clear lines regarding overlap or deceit, by not talking to GB or the group first and by underestimating how fresh and private their breakup still felt, I can see how my actions likely came across as inconsiderate and threatened group trust. If I jumped into dating HR right away, I probably would be viewed as the asshole by most of the group—not for the feelings themselves, but for ignoring the emotional reality everyone was still dealing with. With what I know now, I’d recommend waiting, checking in with GB, and opening up honest conversations before anything becomes public or serious. So to answer the original question: yes, I’d be the asshole right now if I started dating HR without more patience and openness, even if my intentions weren’t bad. Given time and some real transparency, though, I see a path where starting this wouldn’t be an asshole move at all.

[S4] Having read through everyone else's nuanced updates, my position hasn’t fundamentally changed, but I do feel it has solidified around the importance of context—especially timing, communication, and group dynamics. I’m definitely more conscious now of how much the shock to the group, GB in particular, comes less from what I chose and more from how quickly I moved and how little I checked in with people beforehand. Some thoughtful points about not needing to bury real feelings forever just to avoid uneasy moments make sense, but they don’t outweigh the fact that to everyone else, this felt rushed and possibly inconsiderate. While I don’t believe starting to date HR, in itself, makes me inherently the asshole—since there was no overlap or secretive scheming—I do see more clearly now that in the immediate aftermath of GB and HR’s private breakup, any overt moves would feel unnecessarily painful and maybe like a betrayal of friendship priorities. If I look at what the group truly needed for things not to go sideways, it was open, transparent conversations as soon as possible, and patience in letting things cool off. So, to answer directly: at this moment, given how raw things still are, I would be the asshole if I went ahead without more communication and respect for everyone’s headspace, even if my motives weren’t bad. With genuine care and some real conversations first, though, I think things could play out way more smoothly—and eventually not be AH material at all.

[S5] Taking in everyone’s re-examined points and comparing them to my last view, I now feel even more confident in my basic position—this whole situation really centers on handling a sensitive moment with patience and respect. Like most people have echoed, the actual “wrongness” of dating HR isn’t about some universal moral issue, but about how quickly things move and whether conversations happen in the right order. I appreciate that grown-up feelings can naturally emerge, and I still think my intentions weren’t malicious or underhanded. But what really comes out in these discussions is that moving forward before checking in with GB and letting the group process, especially given how private and fresh the breakup was, would (however unintentionally) signal insensitivity or a lack of regard for everyone’s trust. So while I actually feel more understanding toward the “not inherently an AH move” camp, my view hasn’t fundamentally shifted: I’d be the asshole if I rushed into dating HR right now, given the circumstances. Waiting a bit, being transparent, and talking openly—especially with GB—feels not just prudent but necessary if I want to keep the group solid and minimize avoidable hurt. In sum, I’d hold off for now and focus on honest conversations first; in time, with those steps, pursuing HR could be okay without anyone rightfully seeing me as the AH.

[S6] After reading everyone's newest responses and sitting with my own thoughts, I’m seeing even more clearly that the real heart of this issue is timing and transparency—almost everyone agrees that, in principle, adults can pursue new relationships, but the emotional context of a close friend group makes those moves especially sensitive. I still personally believe that jumping into a relationship with HR right now, right after her quiet breakup with GB and without talking things through, would paint me as insensitive if not outright the asshole—mainly because it would feel dismissive of the group’s feelings and GB's position. But the steady chorus around open communication, allowing space for people to adjust, and doing things above board really sticks out to me. I’m taking more to heart now just how much a respectful pause and honest, direct conversations could protect these friendships—even changing the tone from betrayal to mutual understanding. So my bottom line hasn’t changed: right now, it would be selfish of me to start dating HR without letting things settle and talking with GB. But I’m more convinced than ever that my responsibility is about communication and timing, not about romantic feelings themselves. If I handle this the right way—with patience and openness—it doesn’t have to be an "asshole move" at all. For now, though, waiting and reaching out to people comes first.

[S7] Reading everyone’s follow-ups makes me even more conscious of how timing, openness, and group trust are at the heart of whether dating HR now would be an asshole move. I still firmly believe that there’s nothing inherently wrong with two single adults connecting after a breakup—there wasn’t any cheating and my intentions weren’t to hurt anyone. But after seeing how everyone’s landed on the importance of giving GB and the group some space, it’s clear that quickly jumping into things right now would be seen as inconsiderate because people are still coming to terms with the breakup. While my intentions may have been good, the way things unfolded with minimal communication amplified the sense of surprise and disregard for others’ feelings. So my original stance is pretty much the same, just reinforced by all the thoughtful takes here: I’d be the asshole if I pursued things immediately, as it would risk group trust and unnecessarily hurt people close to me. However, if I slow down, prioritize real conversations with GB and the group, and show some patience so everyone can process, pursuing a relationship with HR doesn't have to be an AH move at all. Being thoughtful with timing and transparency is what matters most—and that's really where I need to focus.

[S8] Having absorbed everyone’s most recent input, I feel even more convinced that the heart of this issue isn’t so much about the act of dating a friend’s ex, but the context—the timing after the breakup, how fresh everyone's feelings still are, and especially how the news was shared (or not shared) with the group and with GB in particular. The overwhelming agreement around open communication and patience stands out, and some strong points in newer perspectives made me appreciate just how much trust can hinge on handling transitions carefully, not just ethically. I still maintain that there was no cheating or deliberate hurt, and that genuine feelings for HR aren’t in themselves wrong to pursue. But being honest, I can see that moving forward immediately, without proper conversations or a cooling-off period, dismissed how much the group dynamic—and GB’s feelings—might be shaken by what looks and feels like sudden change. It’s less about morality and more about social sensitivity at a rocky moment. So, my view has softened; the relationship itself isn’t inherently an asshole move, but jumping in without facilitating those sorely needed conversations and space absolutely would be, given the circumstances. I think waiting, talking it out, and showing more empathy would fundamentally change how this feels to everyone involved. I’d be wrong to push ahead “right now,” but with communication and time, I think things could be healthy and above board for all.

[S1] After considering the most recent feedback and really digesting people’s deeper takes—especially about that “breaking point moment” when my girlfriend became upset about the two-person overnight—I see my own perspective developing a little further. Most people seem to agree it was controlling for her to suddenly issue rules and demands, but I also notice a strong strain of opinion pointing to how, when her trust was explicitly shaken, I could have worked harder to show that I cared about her emotional safety and was invested enough in our relationship to at least pause and talk, rather than defaulting straight to “I’m not canceling.” Yes, my original accommodations—inviting, rescheduling, sharing info—matter a lot to me, and I still don’t feel it’s ever healthy to cave to ultimatums about friendships preexisting a romance. But reading how others have described middle grounds I didn’t try (like postponing briefly for one more conversation or being more vulnerable about reassuring her) makes me realize I probably did let my frustration “win out” instead of displaying real empathy in that crucial escalation. That said, I stand by thinking her demands were unhealthy and a major red flag—not just discomfort, but insistence on dictating rules, blocking me, and imposing breakups over disagreement. So overall, while I still don’t think I’m the asshole for not canceling in itself, I am now more clearly seeing that both of us let communication get lost to self-protection and stubbornness. I wish I’d handled things more gently when they got tense. At the end of the day, I keep my stance that refusing to cancel was justified, but I see now my approach could have shown more care—and the way we both responded exposed bigger incompatibilities in how we handle insecurity and conflict.

[S2] After taking in the new comments, especially the ones emphasizing both the context of your longstanding friendship and your efforts to include your girlfriend at each step, I still maintain that this is ultimately an ESH situation, though I’m not quite as firm as before in putting most blame on you. Reading others’ reasoning—including good points about how controlling your girlfriend’s response became, and how difficult it is to stay gentle when ultimatums get swapped for conversation—makes me even more convinced that both sides failed in key ways. I stand by the idea that, given the trip changed into a much more intimate context (overnight, past crush, just you two), it called for much more open and empathetic dialogue; just forging ahead on principle, even transparently, can feel cold or disrespectful in a committed relationship. At the same time, based on how harshly your girlfriend escalated—locking communication, laying down “rules,” and framing it as breakup-or-obedience—I’m more persuaded by those siding with your boundaries, especially after your prior acts of transparency. So bottom line, I haven’t changed my view much: both parties here let fear or defiance get in the way of actual trust-building, and neither handled the escalation as well as they could’ve. You aren’t an outright asshole for protecting a respectful friendship, but you missed a final opportunity to really demonstrate care when it might have mattered most. She crossed the line into controlling. I still think ESH, with an emphasis that the relationship may not stand unless both learn to move past self-protection and engage in honest, gentler conversation when the next tough dilemma arises.

[S3] Having thought more about everyone's latest input, I'm feeling more conflicted, but my perspective has shifted a little further toward the middle. Several people made strong points about how much effort and transparency you showed—inviting your girlfriend, rearranging dates, and making sure she was informed at every turn—which really does matter and makes the accusations of being inconsiderate less fair. Also, I see now that her demands crossed a line from genuine discomfort into outright control, which never tends to foster trust in a relationship. But at the same time, it's clear from other views—and I agree—that *something* more was needed, particularly as the trip suddenly became an intimate situation between you and a former crush. I admit now that simply refusing to cancel may not have addressed the emotional reality for your girlfriend, especially if there were preexisting insecurity or trust issues, and a more collaborative or reassuring approach could have been healthier. Ultimately, I still think your girlfriend’s way of handling this (with ultimatums and extreme "rules") was a red flag, but I also see that your response was too rigid, almost inviting escalation instead of understanding. So, I’m leaning closer now to ESH (everyone sucks here): I can’t say you’re just TA, as your actions came from reasonable motives and respect for boundaries, but you missed a crucial opportunity for empathy; meanwhile, her reaction—demanding you cut off a friendship in this way—was out of bounds. So, both of you played a part in letting the situation blow up, and neither responded in a way that feels truly healthy or fair.

[S4] Having reflected on the newest replies and the way people have evolved in their takes, I find my original view of “not the asshole” remains largely intact, though I recognize with more depth just how messy this was on both sides. The consistent facts don’t change: this was an established friend I’ve always been upfront about, I bent over backwards in planning (inviting my girlfriend, changing the dates, letting her know directly), and the shift to it being just two people really was outside my intent. I see more clearly now that the moment it became a close one-on-one trip with the person I’d once had feelings for, it did deserve a fresh, open check-in—not just assuming everything was still fine on the basis of past reassurance. Where my own approach could have been stronger is in offering more space for my girlfriend’s anxiety and not jumping immediately to draw my own hard lines, since everyone points out how fragile trust can be around these subjects. That said, her attempt to impose rules, demand cancellation, and respond by shutting me out still seems beyond what’s healthy in a partnership. After reading people’s nuanced arguments, I now admit my refusal was justified in the sense of not caving to insecurity-fueled, controlling demands, but my communication was likely too blunt and insufficiently empathetic given the very real stress this caused her. Next time, I’d want to try a more caring re-engagement, not just “standing my ground”—but I still don’t see myself as the asshole for keeping plans that were open, honest, and made in good faith. So, I’m keeping my basic view, but with added humility: my own lack of a reassuring response helped let things spiral, and in that sense, it’s clear neither of us handled the escalation as well as we should have.

[S5] After reading everyone else's thoughtful input, my view has shifted a bit, but I still ultimately land around a soft YTA—with the caveat that the situation is much more complex and there’s mutual fault here. I appreciate all the reminders that you made real efforts to include your girlfriend and that her demands absolutely crossed into controlling territory, which helps me see why so many people feel like refusing to cancel wasn't inherently wrong. However, I remain stuck on the way things played out after the trip changed to just you and the old friend: considering your girlfriend’s discomfort—especially with the history between you and your friend—a more empathetic approach, even just postponing or pausing for a real, calm talk, would have gone a long way. At the same time, your girlfriend escalated the “rules” and ultimatums so quickly that it undermined real dialogue and added to the toxicity. I can now better recognize that this wasn't simply about the trip itself, but about underlying trust, security, and how both of you react to big emotional stumbling blocks—she shouldn’t have tried to control you, but you met her pain with inflexibility rather than comfort. So I’m updating my opinion: you’re a mild TA here, mostly for not finding a better blend of reassurance and autonomy, while your girlfriend’s attempts to dictate and avoid healthy discussion are red flags themselves. Neither of you handled this mess well, and in the end, it seems less like one person being in the wrong than two partners exposing deep incompatibilities in their communication and boundaries.

[S6] Reading through the additional responses and reflecting more on both the nuance people are pointing out and the direct criticism of my handling of the conflict, I’m still leaning toward not being in the wrong (NTA) for refusing to cancel the trip. I was upfront about the plans, included my girlfriend from the start, and did everything I could to reassure her and reschedule for her comfort before the situation changed and left it just two of us. However, the input from others is making me more clearly that, emotionally, this wasn’t just a “reasonable/unreasonable” issue for her: the specific triggers—an overnight trip with someone I once had feelings for—deserved an extra level of empathy and engagement than I brought, even if her later behavior was unhealthy and controlling. I maintain that her final demands crossed a real line, but I do accept now that before it blew up, the calmer, open-hearted talk people suggested may genuinely have been the better move. My decision not to cancel still feels important for my autonomy, yet I now see I was perhaps too rigid in defending my boundaries and insufficiently attentive to how much distress she was honestly showing. So my updated stance: I don’t agree with her response and I don’t think canceling was necessary given my openness and effort—but I regret not trying harder at the most pivotal moment to find softer ground, for my sake and hers. In sum, I’m closer to “not an asshole, but not as considerate as I should have been,” and I definitely recognize this was a lose-lose outcome rooted in mutual communication issues.

[S7] After going over everyone’s follow-ups, I’m still inclined to think YTA—though at this point, it’s very mild, and I recognize the lines are blurred a lot more than I first believed. The core facts are unchanged: you did a lot to include your girlfriend, kept her informed, shifted the trip for her, and the third person’s dropout was outside of your control. I continue to feel, as reinforced by several in this thread, that past romantic tension with your friend, combined with the shift to an unexpectedly intimate two-person overnight, was a real sticking point deserving your girlfriend’s discomfort—and not just “unwarranted jealousy.” I appreciate those who argued for refusing controlling behavior, and I agree that your partner’s demands and her move to ultimatums and blocking were concerning and a sign of larger incompatibilities. However, after reflecting on others’ input, what really stands out is the moment you switched from trying to reassure to standing rigidly on principle instead of letting the situation breathe and addressing her feelings one more time. What some call standing up for boundaries does, in a relationship context—especially with those past dynamics and overall trip changes—read a little like prioritizing stubbornness over connection. At the same time, I can no longer ignore just how far your girlfriend’s reaction slid into controlling, even crossing what I would see as reasonable communication. So, I’m sticking with YTA for not being more patient and constructive about your girlfriend’s emotional boundaries, but given everything, the fault here is shared. If anything, the bigger takeaway is that both of you reached your limits in communicating needs, exposing incompatibilities more than unambiguous wrongdoing.

[S8] After reading the new perspectives and carefully weighing everyone’s input, I’m a bit more aware of how complex this situation is, especially around the emotional dynamics and boundaries at play. I still think the core facts support my position: I was upfront about the trip, invited my girlfriend from the outset, changed dates for her, and only ended up in a two-person situation after someone else canceled. Where my thinking shifts a little is in recognizing—thanks to others’ experiences—that even when you’re being logical or transparent, relationship comfort sometimes needs more than just “doing everything by the book.” Maybe I underestimated how a changed circumstance (an overnight trip alone with someone I’d previously had a crush on) might drive legitimate but difficult feelings for my girlfriend, and that deserved another sincere conversation before I rested on principle. I accept I could’ve been slower to confront and quicker to reassure; at the same time, her escalations into demands and controlling “rules” over my social life still feel far over the line, as multiple people pointed out. I agree the ideal would’ve been to seek a gentler, more collaborative resolution, but I stop short of calling myself TA for refusing to cancel in light of big picture trust and autonomy. Overall, after all this, I maintain I’m not the asshole for holding to my plans, but I admit my handling—the communication and empathy aspects—should have been better. So: mostly NTA, but this has highlighted for me how next time, slowing down for a true heart-to-heart might matter as much as where I set my boundaries.

[S1] Honestly, I think YTA here. You’ve been dating your girlfriend for just over a year and you already live together, which makes her feelings about trust and boundaries important in your relationship. You did invite her to the trip originally, and even rearranged to a date when she’d be away because she said she couldn’t go, which seems considerate.
